lines: Picture one piece of a group of four that keeps failing, over and over.
Does the whole job collapse the very first time that happens, or does the engine give it more chances first?
Give that one troublesome piece enough chances, and run the whole thing.
It eventually comes through, and the entire job finishes normally, as if nothing ever went wrong.
Now give that same piece far fewer chances than it actually ends up needing to succeed.
Does the job still pull through in the end, or does it finally stop trying?
steps.answer: It stops trying, the moment it runs out of chances.

lines: Here's exactly what happens.
The identical piece, failing in exactly the same way as before, but this time the whole job gives up the moment its chances run out.
Here's why that happens.
A set number of extra chances is exactly that: a fixed number, not an unlimited one.
Spend every one of them, and the job dies, even on work that might have eventually come through on its own.
Here's a different kind of question. This time, instead of a piece failing outright, picture a piece of already-finished work simply vanishing partway through.
Does the engine just redo that one missing piece by itself, or does it reach back much further than that?
steps.answer: Much further back. The entire earlier piece of work that produced it gets redone.

lines: Here's exactly what the measurement shows.
Far more than just the one missing piece. The whole earlier stretch of work that produced it gets started over completely, every part of it included.
Here's the reasoning behind that.
Once that earlier work is truly gone, there's no partial patch available to fix it.
The only way to get it back is redoing everything that produced it, not only the one piece that happened to notice it was missing.
Put both kinds of trouble side by side.
One is bounded by a simple count of extra chances. The other drags an entire earlier stretch of work back into motion.
So a limited number of extra chances only buys exactly that, a fixed amount, nothing more.
And losing already-finished work can end up costing far more than the one piece that happened to notice it was gone.
